blocks.text: When more than one capacitor is connected in a circuit to obtain a desired capacitance, the combination behaves as a single equivalent capacitor; its capacitance is the combined capacitance. The two common combinations are parallel and series.

In parallel, one plate of every capacitor is joined to the negative terminal of the battery and the other plate to the positive terminal (Fig 16.8). The potential difference V across each capacitor is the same, but the charge on each depends on its capacitance. The total charge is Q = Q1 + Q2 + Q3. With Q1 = C1 V, Q2 = C2 V, Q3 = C3 V and Q = Ce V: Ce V = C1 V + C2 V + C3 V, so Ce = C1 + C2 + C3 (16.35). When capacitors are connected in parallel, their combined capacitance is the sum of their individual capacitances.

An 80 pF capacitor is charged to 48 V. It is then connected in parallel to an uncharged capacitor, and the potential difference across the combination becomes 30 V. Find the capacitance of the second capacitor. Solution: the charge first is Q1 = C1 V1 = (80 x 10^-12 F)(48 V) = 3840 x 10^-12 C. Afterwards the charge left on C1 is (80 x 10^-12 F)(30 V) = 2400 x 10^-12 C. Charge is conserved, so the charge shifted to C2 is 3840 - 2400 = 1440 x 10^-12 C, and C2 = Q2 / V = 1440 x 10^-12 C / 30 V = 48 x 10^-12 F = 48 pF.

In series the capacitors are joined one after another (Fig 16.9 a): the second plate of C1 is joined to the first plate of C2, and so on, and the first plate of C1 and the last plate of C3 are joined to the battery. The battery gives +Q to the first plate of C1, which induces -Q on its second plate; since that plate is joined to the first plate of C2, +Q appears there, and so on. So each capacitor carries a charge of the same magnitude Q. The potential difference across the combination equals the battery voltage, but it is shared: V = V1 + V2 + V3 (16.36). With V = Q/Ce, V1 = Q/C1, V2 = Q/C2, V3 = Q/C3: Q/Ce = Q/C1 + Q/C2 + Q/C3, so 1/Ce = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3 (16.37). The reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance is the sum of the reciprocals of the individual capacitances; Ce is smaller than the smallest capacitance in the series.

blocks.alt: Left: three capacitors C1, C2 and C3 connected in parallel between the same two wires across a battery; Q = Q1 + Q2 + Q3 and Ce = C1 + C2 + C3. Right: three capacitors C1, C2 and C3 connected one after another in a single loop with a battery; V = V1 + V2 + V3 and 1/Ce = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3.
blocks.caption: Capacitors in parallel and in series (original circuit diagrams after Figs 16.8 and 16.9).
blocks.long_description: In parallel the capacitors share the same voltage and their charges add, so the capacitances add. In series they share the same charge and their voltages add, so the reciprocals add.

blocks.text: Capacitors of 12 uF and 4 uF are connected in series to an 80 V battery. Find (i) the total charge stored and (ii) the potential difference across each. Solution: 1/Ce = 1/12 + 1/4 = (1 + 3)/12 = 1/3, so Ce = 3 uF. (i) Q = Ce V = (3 x 10^-6 F)(80 V) = 2.4 x 10^-4 C. (ii) The same Q is on each: V1 = Q/C1 = 2.4 x 10^-4 / 12 x 10^-6 = 20 V and V2 = Q/C2 = 2.4 x 10^-4 / 4 x 10^-6 = 60 V (20 V + 60 V = 80 V).
